A) There are things that people would be willing to pay for, but many would be unable.

B) There are things that would strongly benefit society in the long run, even increase the economy's health and be a good financial investment, but people are short-sighted and those who could afford it would not pay for all of society to have it.

For example, I'll bring up the example that Libertarians think is a terrible example - roads. Would people build roads if government did not? Of course they would; roads are extremely useful, and well worth the cost to people/communities that could afford to build them. However, people also want to make gains in the short-term. Corporations would build roads, but there would likely be tolls on every major public road. Wealthy communities would likely pave their own roads without tolls. However, major areas of the country, a large number of working class neighborhoods, and a significant percentage of poor people in general would not be able to use roads on a regular basis, if at all. The result of this is lower job opportunities as the working class struggles with transit, a significant blow to the auto industry, a significant blow to the oil industry, a reduction in the available labor market that raises labor prices for employers, etc. This problem becomes everyone's problem.

Now, I think there is some merit to the argument that this is okay, because societies seem to function on survival of the fittest as well. A culture that understands this problem may mend its ways, and find a way to make roads work for everyone, to the benefit of everyone. The cultural zeitgeist may shift, and society may start raising people to think long-term, and voluntarily give up short-term profits for the good of greater society. And cultures/societies that do not learn this lesson will be less suited to prosper, and will likely fade into the background (if not be actively replaced) by societies and cultures that are more suited to long-term thinking. This might be a good thing, in the end.

If you can find a way to convince a whole culture to be responsible, community-driven thinkers that plan for the long-term, congratulations.
